en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. The dialogue between Vāyu and Ādima-mantra, concerning Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the gods, the one worthy of worship, the cause of the earth’s protection, the primordial Guru, the hearing of the Kaṭha-śāstra, the destruction of Hara, the conduct of the ages, the movement through the worlds, the Vedas, the five Pāṇḍavas, the hundred princes, the ocean, the eight Vasus,
the nine planets, the ten Rāvaṇas, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Suns, the thirteen dark nights, the fourteen worlds, and the fifteen lunar days.

The five elements, moving and unmoving, the eighty-four thousand species of living beings, the eight classes of beings, the thirty million deities of the celestial realms and the netherworld (pātāla), those who dwell in the mandalas day and night, the upalas, vipalas, yogas, and muhūrtas— all these,

as well as the deities of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa-devatās), gods, demons, bhūtas, pretas, and rākṣasas, have been summoned and brought here by me through the power of my mantra. They have arrived, having been invoked by me.
Uṣṭra-mūtra (camel urine), aṣṭānabha, ūṣaṇa, elā, nicula, punarnavā,

phalgu, ṛḍiṭha, erīḍa, gadinī, nīpa, śolāya, peya, ghaukaraṇa, mūlavāyu-sūdana, śukra-hara, te-vāyu-rūpa, vāiḍagara, hikkā-karaṇa, pitta-mūtrakṛcchra, aṣṭādaśa-prameha, vāta-golā, phihi, āni, haru, vāha, gāsta, gārdha, aśī, śīluṭī, ḍalūtā, vuvārī, mirigī, kamala, viyuhā, and prā— [these are used for] the treatment of wind-disorders.

The sound of the *vumuvā* drum, the clashing of swords, the cries of the fallen, the lamentations of the survivors, the neighing of horses, the trumpeting of elephants, the roar of the thunderbolt-like bow of the Lord of the Sky (Indra), the twang of the string of the celestial garment-wielder’s (Arjuna) bow— these sounds resounded day and night, filling the quarters of the sky with the splendor of the battle.

O Panacanātha, Caurāsī, Rāna, Sarāpha, Śeṣa, Śaraphadī, Ahīāpīra, Mānerīkī, Śaka, Tivāāda, Makī, Bhaktinārahaibha, Smāntavhaijāyajāhiehi, Piṇḍakuśala, Doṣaphiṭuphiṭu, Svāhā! This is the mantra for blowing upon oneself: Oṃ muratoghāṃ gaḍā vetālajānī morakānane hī śāḍāre nīthilā cikiṭhārā.
Then, having uttered the mantra of the supreme lord of the *pretas*, he caused the earth to tremble with a roar like that of a great mountain or a thundercloud;

he shook the mountains and peaks, and the entire world-system, including the hells, was filled with the sound of "hum" and "phaṭ. He terrified the *vidyādharas* and the *rākṣasas*, reducing them to ashes with his fierce and blazing splendor. Then he—

The Application of the Incense (Ghrādi-prayoga): O Vāghavarāvaikā! *Oṃ*. Untruth is my mother, Śaṅkara is my father; wandering through the quarters of the world, wherever Śaṅkara was born, there my servant (kiṃkara) was born. Wherever the sound of my drum is heard, there the lioness, the heroic mother Vāgheśvarī, who steals the milk, has made her abode. Who is she? Whose is she? Vāgha-ṣur-vvājaṃgalī. *(Note: The text contains archaic or dialectal phonetic spellings and non-standard orthography typical of folk-mantra traditions.)*
Āra-sāryū-lake (the reading of Śārdūla), śarīteṃdu-vāsu-nahari-adhi-āgādhi-āpāṭi-āgadhi-āṭhi-āra-hari,
āra-harī-āla-kālī-ṭhipaṭi-ārayitā-calī-dhārie-are-kauna-kīlau-tare-narasiṃha-vīra-kīlau,
kahu-kavana-kavana-kīlau-gāyaka-jāyā-bhai-sika-jāyā-bheḍīka-jāyā-cheḍīka-jāyā-ghoḍīka-jāyā.
The fierce fire of the great Śiva’s matted locks burns away all sins; the rags of Gaurī-Pārvatī burn away all sins;
Hanumān, Varāha, and Bhīma likewise drive away all sin. Furthermore:
the enemy is like a flower, the mountain is like a cloth; as a hero alone [removes] the head, so too does he remove the white garment from the forest of his enemies, casting it aside.

The Lord of the Revā river appeared; Mahādeva and Gaurī Pārvatī were there, as were Hanumān, the various ascetics, Cammārī, Ājñāvāk, Sāvācā, and Cūka. Thus the Guru’s power was established, and my devotion shone forth. The Lord of Mantras said: "Furthermore, wherever you sit, you shall speak; go to the upper country, and let there be no obstacle for you. Let there be no obstacle to your livelihood; let there be no obstacle to your face, and let your face be victorious over all others."

Hua-vadha-utha-uva-dhaucha-ri-pava-vadhaute-ree-puchha-vadhou-na-vadhaute-me-ree-a-nind-ra-rudra-kee-a-nava-jru-thu-vadhee-udu-duhaee-mahaadeva-parvatee-ke-dhari-kankara-vera-pachhita-rita-raphaaraiveecha-vaithe. Anyacha: Daandala-valaka-muha-vikaraala-dheera-rachhanda-ahaara-rama-deva-mela-chaat-jahuva-gharoja. In the battle, the enemy was struck down; the foot was wounded, and the enemy was questioned as he was being struck. He was not struck by me, nor by Indra or Rudra. The nine-fold weapon was struck, and the milk was drawn; Mahadeva and Parvati held the staff and the *kankara* (pebble). Having recited the *taraphaara* (the cry of victory), he sat upon the waves. Furthermore: The fierce-faced child of the staff-holder, the courageous one in the meter, the necklace, Rama the God—having met, they were all swallowed by the mouth of the ocean.
*Sātāṭha*, and furthermore, *mahādevakekūkuralūṭekānamerainikaṭāvotamahādevakīāni*—three tālas;
and furthermore, *vāghavāghatumavaḍavānāṭhāṭhīlahugarīdehupacānāgaurīśaṃkarapochatu*—I speak, *mahāhicchāḍijāhukośapāṃca*—thus three tālas; then the mantra for the *vigga-vavarāva-kauma*: *vigulitī*.
Yutāka-pade-lā-nihā-hai-nātha-kai-āna-mero-pahare-vaiṭhai-bhīmam-ārahu-vigajo-cāpaisīma. Furthermore:

Miśrita-mantra vāgha-vāgu-la-sarpa-coracāriu-vādhaue-kaiṭhaura-dharatīmātā-ākāśa-pitā-rakṣa-rakṣa Śrī-Parameśvarī-Kālikā-vācā-mahādevaka-duhāī. Thus, three claps [of the hand]. This concludes the section on protection against sound.

The mantra for warding off calamities: *Samudra-samudra-medīya-dāya-mekū-kūpame-kuṇḍa-kuṇḍame-jahati-cale-hari-hāpare-calāvata-calā-hanumanta-varāvata-calā-bhīma-gaurā-vārā-lā-īśvara-bhāji-maṭhame-jāya-gaurāvai-ṭhiduvāre-nahāya-ṭhapakai-navuṃda-parai-navolā-rājā-indrakī-duhāī-me-bhakta-gurukī-śakti-phura-mantrī*. [This is a protective incantation invoking the power of the ocean, the mountains, the wells, the ponds, the fierce Hanumān, the Lord, the Maṭha, the King, Indra, the Guru, and the devotees.]

With the voice of a serpent-king, [uttering] three *tālas*: "O Serpent! O Serpent Bhadra! Go far away! O Great Sage born of Jaya! Remember the words of Āstīka! Having remembered the words of Āstīka, that serpent who does not depart shall have his head split into a hundred pieces, like the fruit of a tree falling upon a thorn. At the time of sleep, having struck three *tālas*, [one should recite]: "Now, the boar, the mouse, the *nāhāīka*, and the five-knot [serpent]..."

The field of Haradī is like a heap of unhusked grain; the field of Rāvā is like a heap of excellent gold. The field of Mūsāghara is like a heap of sesame seeds; the field of Khetasejāya is like a heap of rice. The field of Ihāseje is like a heap of barley; the field of Udurāvathi is like a heap of beans. The field of Hāseha is like a heap of lentils; the field of Duharana is like a heap of chickpeas. The field of Hāsehanumaṃta is like a heap of peas; the field of Laiāvai is like a heap of vetches. The field of Vādhikhetasā is like a heap of excellent wheat; the field of Suvarajāya is like a heap of fine rice. The field of Petachāḍi is like a heap of millet; the field of Vāherabhūmi is like a heap of wild rice. The field of Jāyaduhāī is like a heap of *hanumaṃta* beans; the field of Kai is like a heap of excellent *suvara* beans; the field of Mūsā is like a heap of *jāī* beans. Furthermore, the field of Citaphaṇī is like a heap of *gaṇa* beans; the field of Cūhā is like a heap of *cūhā* beans.
The Lord of Lanka, Ravana, whose body was as dark as a rain-cloud, who wore yellow garments, and who was the son of the Earth (Musha), was killed by Hanuman.

O Hanuman, you went to Lanka; who else could have stayed there? Who else could have gone? Only the son of the Wind (Hanuman) knows the mantra; he alone goes when it is recited. You are on his head, you are in his belly; you have gone to Kaṭau, to Ānaka, to Kheta, to Gaurī, to Pārvatī, and you have gone to Mahādeva. Furthermore, [the mantra] is *sūka-śanī*.
The dense forest of my ears has been filled by the sound of the *moreha* drum; having abandoned the groves of the city of Mores, I have come to this forest.

Having cast off all worldly desires, I have taken up the supreme weapon of the mantra. The sixty-four *yoginīs* have arrived as my protectors, wearing iron armor and providing me with protection. May the power of my guru, Śrī Gorakhnāth, and my devotee Hanumān, the hero, provide me with protection.
With his hand he grasps a sword; with a single stroke he cuts off heads like ships.
With a thousand strokes of the edge of his blade, he severs nine hundred and ninety-nine thousand lives. O Śrī Gorakh Rāva, he is the protector of the imperishable. Furthermore, he has arrived;
at the time of cutting, he is like sesame seeds in sesame oil. He sits by the side of the Gujarīs; he wears a garment of rags and knows no fear. Month after month, he strikes blow after blow.
The stream of the Āṣāḍha month, which is like a river of nectar for the ears of the world, flows from the cloud that is the Lord Goraṣarāva;
it bursts forth and provides protection. O Lord, when you appear in the sky, how can the clouds not be struck down?
When you are in the month of Āṣāḍha, all streams are bound by your mantra; abandon this iron-like head of yours, for Umā and Śaṅkara have taken refuge at your feet. Come, do not cause us grief.

O Lord Mahādeva, you who hold the bow that shatters the pride of the gods and asuras, who are fierce in tearing apart the hosts of demons, and who bear the burden of deluding the world—protect me on my path! O Upholder of the Bow, may your fierce power not fail; may it be firm for me. My refuge is the power of the Guru of my devotion, and the feet of the Siddha Guru. Furthermore, the Mother, the Father, and the Guru are the Upholders of the Bow, the Upholders of the Bow.
By the mere touch of this weapon in the hand, Hanumān became invincible; by the grace of Śrī Gorakṣanātha, he was protected from all dangers.

By Narasiṃha Siṃhakera, the path of death was destroyed. He performed the paralyzing of fire and the binding of ignorance. He was a blind man to the terrifying blows of the crores of Yama’s messengers, yet he was the Lord of the World (Īśvara) to his own brothers. He fought with those who were deluded, and he himself became enlightened.
O Numaṃta-vādha, O Upāni-huja, O Yabavanaika-bhava-tasamada-mātī-hāthī-vādha, O Hovaishaṃdara-vādha, O Nārāyaṇa-sāṣī!
May the power of my devotion to the Guru be manifest; may the mantra-sound arise. Furthermore:
O Agni-vādha, O Vāhana-vādha, O Kulyāhāhā-vādha, O Vīcakaiva-ṣacāri-hukhūṭa-vaiśaṃdara-vādha, O Trāsata-sama-rābhāī! May it be bestowed upon me. May it be realized.
The Lord of the Earth became cool; the fire was extinguished; the heat of the flames and other fires subsided. By the water from his hand, the tongue [of the fire] was quenched by the waters.
At the command of the heroic Hanumān, that fire-vīra was shattered. O Vīra Hanumān, your power is great; my devotion is even greater than your power.
Thus spoke the Lord of the Three Worlds. Oil became solidified like water; oil became like water; the fire-pit became like a lotus-pond; and the five *pūtaka* spears became like chariots.

With hands and feet as unsteady as the edge of a furrow, they gaze upon the fire; their eyes are parched, and they are struck by the arrows of the divine Cupid. Others say that he who recites [this] conquers the enemy. Furthermore: "The forest is afflicted, the earth is afflicted, and the throat is afflicted;
O Lord, grant me relief! Grant me coolness in the forest, even if Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the Goddess Kāmākṣā themselves were my refuge."

The path becomes impassable due to the water of the *duhāī* (the rainy season). In this context, the mantra for extinguishing fire is as follows: "O Fire, you are my protector; may you be my refuge. Even if another's body is difficult to attain, O Narasiṃha, may I obtain the matted locks (*jaṭā*) of the one who is difficult to reach. [Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Quelling of Fire for Pretas and Others," in the *Śrīsāvaratantra*, within the *Mantrasaṃgraha* concerning the life-story of Bhānumatī and others. Now...

Regarding the types of fever and other ailments, first is the ritual application for Ḍākinī: [The mantra is] *ṭonājhāraikāmaṃtra somaśanīcarabhauma agārīka hācalī deṣiadhipārī cārighaṃṭā vajūke vāraṭonahi vādhausoma duvāra uttaravādhau koī dānavatāī dakṣiṇavāṃdhau kṣetrapāla cāri vidyāvāṃdhikaidevaje se svabhavaraṃbhamādighila bhavaragaṇagaṃdharva*. [This refers to the specific mantras and deities associated with the various directions and planetary influences. (Note: The provided text contains a highly corrupted or non-standard transcription of Sanskrit mantras and deity names. The translation above attempts to render the literal sequence as it appears, while acknowledging the technical nature of the content.)
The demon Cālu was subdued by Śiva; the yogi Uttarāpathaka was subdued; King Vāsuki of Pātāla was subdued; Rāmacandra subdued Keśinī;

the hero Īśvara Mahādeva subdued Duhāī; Gaurī Pārvatī subdued Jauṭonāra. By reciting this *piṇḍamantra* and blowing upon it, one subdues Jauṭonāra. Furthermore, this is the *ākarṣaṇa-mantra* for bringing Jauṭonāra under one's control.
Lonāsalonā Yoginī, O Vādhūṭī! Bring [the power] here; Śaṣī Milipāpa, Kavana Deśaka, Kavana Vaiphi!

O Radiant One, O Flower-like One! May victory be yours! O Vāsateū, O Fruit-like One! Come to me! O Pārśvakāvara Devī, by the power of your devotion, the Lord of Mantras has spoken. "Jvara, Jhārai, Kāūṭha, Ajamerikā, King Jaipāla."

Jaipāla, Kīra, Nīma, Malayāgiri, Sātaputra, Sātaputrīya, Taptaputra, Khākhāra, Khākhora, Ekajara, Nijara, Caitha-jvara, Rātrijvara, Varadivasa-jvara, Khālī, Khuliya, Unmatha, Vāyujvara, Jūḍī, Huphuṭanī, Andhā, Śīśī, Bhāju, Bhāju-pāpī, Rāja-jaipālaka, Cakrāvaika, Kaṭikuṭi, Samu...

With the mantra: "drakhāravahāvairājājaipālakaiduhāījopāpīrahai," one should begin at the head and proceed down to the feet, facing west while looking at the sacrificial offering (havya), and standing facing east, perform the striking with black gram (māṣa). As the mantra is recited, the fever departs. Furthermore: "ekajaraduijaratijarālohāgahaṃtideśāvasatiu" [The single old one, the two old ones, the old iron, they seize the country and dwell there].

"O King of the city of Jenapura, O King Jaipāla! May the fevers caused by *kaiduha* and *ijauja* depart. Furthermore: Om, salutations to Ajai-pālaka! May the fevers caused by *kaiduha* and *ijauja* be destroyed! O Mahādeva! May the fever caused by *kaiduha* flee! The Lord of Mantrins said: "One should write this on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) with saffron (*sātava*), place it in a vessel, and wear it around the neck; it is the destroyer of fever. Furthermore: "In the northern region of the ocean, there is a Vānara named Kumuda. By the mere remembrance of him, the fever departs to the ten directions in the netherworld (*rasātala*)."

One should offer water for drinking with the single mantra: *Oṃ Agastyāya namaḥ*. May that Agastya be pleased—he who, gazing upon the strength of Prajāpati, assumed the form of a pitcher and grew like a fierce bull; he by whom Vātāpi was consumed and the great Asura Vātāpi was likewise devoured; he by whom the ocean was dried up. [May] Agastya, Kumbhakaraṇa, Sami, and Vaḍavānala [be propitiated]. *Ā...* (The text appears to be truncated here).
Hārapatī, Nātha, Smara, Ghaṭa, Vṛkodara, Āṣīphūlī, Māḍājhāra, Eka-sarpa, Atisrasukanyā, Cyavana, Śatrughna, and Svastimat—
by the mere remembrance of these, eye disease is destroyed. Paṭhika, Pīnī, Kāchīṭāmāra, Vāra-uṭhī,
Āṃṣijhāra, Ekā-vane, Viāīvānarī, Jahājāī, Hanumān, Āṣīpīḍā, Kaṣāvarī, Gahi-hātha, and Tailā.

The Lord of Mantrins, whose power was heavy with the ashes of his birth and who was a master of devotion to Meru, spoke: "O King Jaipāla, the one who delights you, the one who delights you—where is that one? O King, where is he? Is it the flame of the fire-sticks, or the sound of the drum of devotion? Is it the roar of the ocean at the edge of the world, or the cry of the peacock? Is it the sound of the conch, or the voice of the one who has attained tranquility?"

In this place, the waters of the Uttarāha, Rājāha, Jaipālaka, Kāka, Hārapānī, Bharaha, Unadeṣa, Pāvāvalī, Goḍiyā, Melā, Ujāla, and Taṅkaṇa flow; here, one should worship the Lord Mahādeva, who dwells in the form of a well. Furthermore, when the goddess Kālī laughs with "ki-laki-lā" sounds, Līlādevī, Vāsudeva, Añjanī, and Hanumāna dwell there; by striking the heart [of the deity], one cures head-splitting pain, headache, and all types of migraines. This is the mantra.

Listen! The garland of skulls, the white skull-topped staff, the entrails, the snakes, the lion-skin garment, the thick clouds, the roar, the terrifying house, the drum-beating, the great dance, the vajra, listen!

The laughter, the multitude of clouds, the fear, the gnashing of teeth, the fire-blowing, the fire-voice-blowing, the terrifying voice-blowing, the iron-chain-blowing, the thunderbolt-hail, the thunderbolt-storm, the destroyer of wealth, the tamer of the wicked—listen to this great [sound]!

The affliction caused by the *devakā* (demons) is cured by reciting mantras, by blowing [over the patient] with a vessel containing water, and by the application of *vārasāta*. The affliction caused by *hūka* (spirits) is cured at will by the mantra.

The affliction caused by *sumeru-parvata* (mountain-demons), *paralona* (foreign spirits), *caṃmārī* (plague-spirits), *soneka* (gold-eaters), *surāpī* (wine-drinkers), *hukavu* (snakes), *kavāha* (wind-spirits), *vilārī* (cats/spiders), *dharaṇī* (earth-spirits), *nālī* (reed-spirits), *kūṭikūṭi* (deceptive spirits), and those who drink the salt-water of the ocean is cured by this mantra.
The Lord of Mantras said: "By this mantra, one should touch the ring finger and the thumb..."

Eleven times [recite] the ear-root mantra of Hanumān: "Vanahiḍāṭhīvānarī tauḍāṭhe hanumāna kaṃkhavilāro vāṃdhī thamailā kanaśūra asavajāya rāmacandra kaiva cana pānī pathaṭhu jāya. By reciting this mantra, one becomes like a lion among elephants; one becomes a tiger among deer; one becomes a snake among kachuhīs. Who can capture him? Who can bind him? No one at all. He is the son of the Wind-god, dwelling on Mount Kailāsa. No one can seize him. No one can bind him. No one at all.

Lākara, bahusāri, patravāyu, vāṭhika, śāripatra, khāuka, kāṅkara, bahu-aṣṭa-uttara-saivyādhika, āṭikai, rāvana, kaiśīśa, daśabhujā, vīśavara, vaṭivāyu, golāka, chuhīcana-gāvāyu, gulma, sabhehi, piṇḍarahaitau, mahādeva, gaurā-pārvatī, nīlakaṇṭha, unonāca, mārīka—these are the duhāīs. Furthermore: high and low, enemies and kinsmen, they all fall under the shadow of the sun. *Note: This text appears to be a fragment of a medical or astrological manual (possibly related to *piṇḍa* calculations or planetary influences) written in an archaic or regional Prakrit/Hindi dialect. The terms listed likely refer to specific diseases, planetary positions, or astrological configurations.*

Lichāra, arevī, dhatūrā, apāmārga, lahasun, kār̤hā, rūṣakāṭikā, karavī, elā, karavī-elā, kākarava, sarpapattrakhāu, gāḍai, aisāripattrakhāukā, kākarava, varavaṭavā, yugolā, canagā, kachuhīvā, yugulmī,
savakāṭi, kūṭi, samudrakhaṇḍa, vahāvamorī, siddhigurukai, pāvaśaraṇa, athaḍā, phājhārai, kāvādarūpara.
The *Dohā* of Gokula Cāmara Sonekachūrī, who was like a crest-jewel among the *Dalavādalas* and was dependent on others;
the *Dohā* of Jhāroḍāvā Kāṭosaraphūla, whose heart was pained by the separation from his beloved; the *Dohā* of Īśvara Mahādeva, the husband of Gaurā Pārvatī, which is the *Phura-mantra*.
Īśvara said: Furthermore—O you sons of Ḍāvāka, O sons of Kālī, O you who are as sharp as the edge of a sword! O King, this is my counsel.

The *piṇḍa* is offered by those who have been liberated from the womb; Hanumān has sung this in two verses. Furthermore, it is proclaimed in the *Vādarūpa*: "In the cow-pen (*gokula*), the young bull dwells;
he is the one who cuts through the multitude of swords in the form of worldly existence. This is the secret of the *piṇḍa*, which Mahādeva told to Gaurī and Pārvatī in two verses.

O Hero, even if you behold this secret of the *piṇḍa*, it is like a mixture of *jambīra* fruits; the mantra is not recited here, nor is it uttered, nor is it sought after, nor is it placed at the site of the *vilārī*. It is the *elāpā*.

The *cavāṇa*, *mohi*, *bhairava*, *delā*, *kaṃkhā*, *vilārī*, *palaṭijā*, *hughara*, *apane*, *rājā*, *manerī*, and *kaiduhāī*—these twelve *guruka* (heavy) *duhāīs* were joined together. There was no *kāma-mantra* here; rather, it was the *cāla-mantra*. "Leave Laṅkā! Vibhīṣaṇa, depart! Go quickly, go quickly! Thus the *mantra* was chanted. Then, in anger, the *mantra* of King Jayapāla Sāgarakhāna was uttered: "O King Vaṃṭa, run, run to the bank! And there it remained.
